unclear if this is allowed under the license, and no further feedback was received from copyright holders.
I have concerns, but happy to hear any evidence to the contrary.
Moving to -2 on account of this contradicting the SPDX advice

We might need someone at a higher pay-grade to approve this, as I believe IBM have specific requirements about the format of the copyright notice.

More generally though, the apache license states:

> You must retain, in the Source form of any Derivative Works
> that You distribute, all copyright, patent, trademark, and 
> attribution notices from the Source form of the Work, 
> excluding those notices that do not pertain to any part of the Derivative Works

and it doesn't seem to me like this is retaining that notice.

> You must retain, in the Source form of any Derivative Works
that You distribute, all copyright, patent, trademark, and
attribution notices from the Source form of the Work,

We retain the notice but in a different form. For example if we changed the file encoding or made a screenshot of the file, *the notice is also retained,
but not byte-for-byte.*

> "Source" form shall mean the preferred form for making modifications, including but not limited to software source code, documentation source, and configuration files.

If we view a patch to be a derived work from the parent commit, the source form may be different, right? So if the new source form is to use SPDX, the representation is different but the notice is in the source form of the derived work.

I have some viewpoint on `SPDX-License-Identifier`. We make it clear, without doubt, in machine-readable form, what is the license of this file. All attributions and copyright holders are still present.

There is an lwn article about SPDX usage.
https://lwn.net/Articles/739183/

> as I believe IBM have specific requirements about the format of the copyright notice.

@spinler@us.ibm.com can you help out here, is it okay for IBM?

> We retain the notice but in a different form. For example if we changed the file encoding or made a screenshot of the file, the notice is also retained,
but not byte-for-byte.

That is clearly different, your examples are a format conversion, not a change in the content. Arguing that the representation of the full copyright notice is still present in this file is disingenuous.

... and, in my understanding, the presence of that full copyright text is the requirement for clearly applying a license to a source text.

> We make it clear, without doubt,

I think you will have a difficult time arguing this. The clarity is reduced, and is no longer in the form that a typical counsel will argue is necessary.

That said, if you have actual legal counsel advising this is okay, and the ToF recognise that advice, I will happily be corrected on this.

The ASF have actual requirements on the presence of the full header on their own contributions:

  https://www.apache.org/legal/src-headers.html

and have specific advice for applying the license:

  https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.html#apply

> There is an lwn article about SPDX usage.
https://lwn.net/Articles/739183/

Yes, that's good for the kernel context, but only covers the SPDX-License-Identifier header, not the FileCopyrightText header. Note that the kernel requirements still require a copyright & attribution header in conjunction with the SPDX metadata.

I am 100% in support of adding the SPDX headers, but they should be in conjunction to the standard header.

Nothing in the REUSE specs seems to require removing existing texts.

In fact, the SPDX advice states:

> SPDX IDs are intending to express information about licenses. Copyright notices ‐
> statements about who owns the copyright in a file or project ‐ are outside the
> scope of SPDX short-form IDs.
>
> Therefore, you **should not** remove or modify existing copyright notices in files 
> when adding an SPDX ID.

\- https://spdx.dev/learn/handling-license-info/ , emphasis in original.

For context on the IBM side: ISTR that the required form included the © symbol, at least. This is one of the preferred formats of the RESUSE spec.

I asked about this on reuse mailing lists reuse@lists.fsfe.org and got following response (archives seem to require an account, but it's a public list so I'm re-posting here)

```
Hi Alexander,

I don't have a good answer for this.

MPL-2.0 has a FAQ[1] which says:

> Q27: Can I use a machine-readable header in my source code files to indicate that the file is under the MPL?
>
> Use of a standards-compliant, machine-readable license metadata header in source code files can be compliant with the notice-related goals and requirements of MPL 2.0.
>
> MPL 2.0 recommends the use of the specific text in Exhibits A or B in order to provide consistency for recipients of source code. However, the license was drafted with the understanding that not all technical communities may be able to, or wish to, use the header in the recommended manner. In particular, Exhibit A notes that it may not be "desirable" to include the standard header in all files, and describes some alternative mechanisms.
>
> As a result, use of a machine-readable mechanism, such as a Software Package Data Exchange® (SPDX) ID, can meet the requirements of the license.
>
> Where a relevant technical community's stated policy is to require such machine-readable license metadata, such as those communities that recommend use of SPDX IDs or the REUSE project's licensing data specification, we recommend following that community's practice.

On a purist technicality, this FAQ answer contradicts the license text
in the same way as you have described in your e-mail message, and
somewhat acknowledges this. But Mozilla decide to interpret the license
a little more generously here.

You could _probably_ safely do the same with Apache, but I am not a
lawyer, and if I were, I wouldn't be your lawyer.

Essentially you can ask yourself:

1. Would the original author object to your changing of the header?
2. If they object, would it be a severe upset?
3. If the upset is severe, is it severe enough to start legal
proceedings against you? (And do you care to 
4. If they start legal proceedings against you, would they win?

If at any stage the answer is 'yes', that's a sign that you may not
want to do this. But _if_ the author objects, you can just write
another patch to fix it, and they'll probably be nice about it.

I hope this helps.

Yours with kindness,
Carmen

[1]: https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/MPL/2.0/FAQ/
```

The response is not conclusive, i am just listing it here for reference since it has a few good points.

@spinler@us.ibm.com can you confirm/deny it it's okay on IBM side to make this change?

If IBM has specific requirements on their copyright notice then maybe they also have a lawyer to help clarify this.

I wouldn't even know where to track that down, but I can try.  Looking at IBM's own projects at github.com/IBM most projects don't seem to use source file copyrights at all, and they're MIT & apache from what I've seen.
